desc:
Place n queens on an n × n board so that no two queens attack each other (no shared row, column or diagonal). A placement is written as an array cols of length n: cols[r] is the 0-based column of the queen in row r.

Many placements can exist. Return the lexicographically smallest one, comparing cols[0] first, then cols[1], and so on. If no placement exists, return an empty array.

n = 4  →  [1, 3, 0, 2]
n = 6  →  [1, 3, 5, 0, 2, 4]
n = 3  →  []
hints: Every row holds exactly one queen, so decide row by row which column to use.
A queen at (r, c) blocks column c, diagonal r - c and anti-diagonal r + c. Remember these three sets (or three bitmasks) while you recurse, and undo them when you backtrack.

Try the columns of each row from left to right and stop the whole search at the first complete placement. The first one found by this order is automatically the lexicographically smallest. If the search finishes without success, return [].
editorial: Depth-first search over rows. In row r try every column c that is not under attack, place the queen, and recurse into row r + 1; if the recursion fails, remove the queen and try the next column. Attacks are tracked in O(1) with a column set and two diagonal sets, or with three bitmasks where the diagonal masks are shifted by one position at every row.

Because rows are filled in order and the columns of each row are tried in increasing order, the very first complete placement found is the lexicographically smallest one, so the search can stop immediately. For n = 2 and n = 3 the search exhausts all options and returns the empty array. The worst case is exponential, but the pruning makes the first solution appear after only a modest number of steps for the sizes allowed here.
time: O(n!) worst case, much less in practice
